::: {.session-lead}
We have learned how to measure a health inequality within one country. But is
an inequality observed in Switzerland **large or small**? To answer that
question, we need comparison. In this session, you will examine how health
levels and health inequalities vary across countries and over time using the
European Social Survey (ESS) and the International Social Survey Programme
(ISSP).
:::

## About this session

This is a **guided self-study session**. There is no regular classroom
meeting. Work through this page in the order presented and complete the
exercises as you go.

The session builds directly on Session 2.

In Session 2, our basic question was:

> **How does health vary by education in Switzerland?**

We now extend this in two directions:

1. **Across countries:** Is the educational health inequality observed in
   Switzerland larger or smaller than in other countries?
2. **Across time:** Has the magnitude of health inequality changed?

The empirical logic remains familiar:

> **Define → measure → compare → quantify → visualise → interpret**

But comparison introduces an additional challenge:

> **Are we actually comparing the same thing?**

## Learning objectives

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- compare health levels across countries;
- compare the magnitude of health inequalities across countries;
- distinguish between **population health** and **health inequality**;
- compare health inequalities across survey waves;
- recognise basic problems of cross-national and over-time comparability;
- use grouped summaries in R to construct country-level estimates;
- visualise variation in health inequalities across countries; and
- formulate a comparative empirical question suitable for your own project.

## From a national estimate to a comparative question

Suppose we find that:

> 80% of highly educated respondents in Switzerland report good or very good
> health, compared with 70% among respondents with low education.

The absolute educational health inequality is:

$$
80\%-70\%=10 \text{ percentage points}
$$

Is **10 percentage points** a large inequality?

By itself, the number does not tell us.

If comparable inequalities are only 2 or 3 percentage points in most other
countries, Switzerland would appear relatively unequal.

If gaps of 15 or 20 percentage points are common elsewhere, the same Swiss
estimate would appear comparatively small.

This illustrates one of the main purposes of comparative research:

::: {.definition}
**Comparison provides a benchmark.**

It allows us to ask whether an observed pattern is common, unusual, stable or
changing.
:::

## Three comparative questions

Comparative health-inequality research often asks three different questions.

### 1. Do countries differ in average health?

For example:

> Is good self-rated health more common in Switzerland than in Germany?

This concerns **population health levels**.

### 2. Do countries differ in health inequality?

For example:

> Is the educational gap in self-rated health larger in Switzerland than in
> Germany?

This concerns the **distribution of health within countries**.

### 3. Do health inequalities change over time?

For example:

> Has the educational health gap in Switzerland become larger or smaller over
> the past decade?

This concerns **change in inequality**.

These questions should not be confused.

::: {.callout-important}
### A healthy country is not necessarily an equal country

A country can have:

- high average health and large health inequalities;
- high average health and small health inequalities;
- low average health and large health inequalities; or
- low average health and small health inequalities.

Comparing average health and comparing health inequality are therefore
different analytical tasks.
:::

## A simple example

Consider two hypothetical countries:

| Country | Low education | High education | Absolute gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Country A | 70% | 85% | 15 pp |
| Country B | 80% | 90% | 10 pp |

Country B has higher levels of good health in **both groups**.

It also has a **smaller absolute educational health inequality**.

But now consider:

| Country | Low education | High education | Absolute gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Country C | 60% | 70% | 10 pp |
| Country D | 80% | 90% | 10 pp |

Countries C and D have identical absolute inequalities, but very different
levels of population health.

This is why comparative analysis should usually report:

1. the health level of each group;
2. the measure of inequality; and
3. the country context in which the inequality occurs.

## Comparability is not automatic

Before comparing countries, we need to ask whether our measures mean
approximately the same thing in each case.

Several problems can arise.

### Question wording

The wording of a health question may differ between survey programmes.

Even small wording differences can affect responses.

### Response categories

Two surveys may both measure self-rated health but offer different response
categories.

A binary indicator such as “good health” may therefore not be constructed in
exactly the same way.

### Education

National education systems differ considerably.

International surveys therefore use harmonised classifications to make
educational attainment more comparable across countries.

Even these harmonised measures are approximations.

### Survey composition

Countries can differ in:

- age structure;
- education levels;
- migration;
- labour-market participation;
- urbanisation; and
- many other characteristics.

A raw difference between countries may therefore reflect differences in who
was surveyed as well as differences in the relationship we are interested in.

### Time

Comparisons across survey waves require additional care.

Question wording, coding, survey modes, participating countries and weighting
procedures can change.

::: {.callout-note}
### The practical rule

For this session, we will compare observations **within the same survey
programme** wherever possible:

- ESS with ESS;
- ISSP with ISSP.

We will not treat ESS and ISSP estimates as if they formed one seamless time
series.
:::

## Part I: Comparing countries using the ESS

We begin with the European Social Survey.

Our first comparative research question is:

::: {.definition}
**How does educational inequality in self-rated health vary across European
countries?**
:::

We will use ESS Round 11.

The basic strategy is:

> **Calculate health by education within each country → calculate the
> educational health gap within each country → compare those gaps**

## Step 1: Load the packages

Open RStudio and load the packages used in Session 2:

```r
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(countrycode)
```

If you have not installed them before, install them once:

```r
install.packages(c(
  "haven",
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2",
  "scales",
  "countrycode"
))
```

## Step 2: Import ESS Round 11

The data are stored in the common project-level `data` folder.

From the Session 3 folder, import the dataset using:

```r
ess11 <- read_dta("../../data/ESS11.dta")
```

Inspect the dimensions:

```r
dim(ess11)
```

And examine the country variable:

```r
table(ess11$cntry)
```

Unlike Session 2, we **do not filter to Switzerland**.

The country dimension is now central to our analysis.

## Step 3: Create readable country names

The ESS uses two-letter country codes.

For graphs, it is useful to create country names:

```r
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    country = countrycode(
      cntry,
      origin = "iso2c",
      destination = "country.name"
    )
  )
```

Check the result:

```r
table(ess11$country, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Step 4: Construct the health outcome

We again use self-rated health.

First inspect the original variable:

```r
table(ess11$health, useNA = "ifany")
```

Create the binary indicator used in Session 2:

```r
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    health_good = case_when(
      health %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      health %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
```

Check the new variable:

```r
table(ess11$health_good, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Step 5: Construct comparable education groups

We use the harmonised ESS education variable `eisced`.

Inspect it first:

```r
table(ess11$eisced, useNA = "ifany")
```

For this exercise, we collapse the harmonised categories into three broad
groups.

```r
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      eisced %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Low",
      eisced %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Medium",
      eisced %in% c(6, 7) ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
```

Make the ordering explicit:

```r
ess11 <- ess11 %>%
  mutate(
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
    )
  )
```

Inspect the distribution:

```r
table(ess11$education, useNA = "ifany")
```

::: {.callout-note}
### Why simplify education?

The harmonised ESS education variable contains more detail than we need for
this exercise.

Collapsing it into **low, medium and high education** makes the comparative
pattern easier to see.

This is a substantive analytical choice rather than a property of the data.
In independent research, you should always document how such groups were
constructed.
:::

## Step 6: Compare average health across countries

Before analysing inequality, examine overall health levels.

Calculate the proportion reporting good or very good health in each country:

```r
country_health <- ess11 %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good))
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(good_health))
```

Inspect the result:

```r
country_health
```

Convert the estimates to percentages if you prefer:

```r
country_health <- country_health %>%
  mutate(
    good_health_pct = good_health * 100
  )
```

Now visualise the result:

```r
ggplot(
  country_health,
  aes(
    x = reorder(country, good_health),
    y = good_health
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Self-rated health across European countries",
    subtitle = "European Social Survey, Round 11"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

<!-- EXERCISE -->

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 1: Compare health levels

Use the table and graph to answer:

1. Which countries report the highest levels of good health?
2. Which report the lowest?
3. Where is Switzerland located?
4. How large is the difference between the highest- and lowest-ranking
   countries?
5. Does this analysis tell us anything yet about **health inequality within
   countries**?
:::

The answer to the final question is **no**.

So far, we have compared average health.

We have not yet compared how health is distributed between social groups.

## Step 7: Calculate health by education within countries

We now calculate good health separately for the three educational groups
within every country.

```r
health_by_country_education <- ess11 %>%
  filter(!is.na(country), !is.na(education)) %>%
  group_by(country, education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Inspect the result:

```r
health_by_country_education
```

For Switzerland alone:

```r
health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(country == "Switzerland")
```

This should look familiar from Session 2.

The difference is that we have now repeated the same calculation for all ESS
countries.

## Step 8: Visualise educational gradients across countries

One way to inspect the result is to plot health by education for each country.

```r
ggplot(
  health_by_country_education,
  aes(
    x = education,
    y = good_health,
    group = country
  )
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Educational gradients in self-rated health",
    subtitle = "European Social Survey, Round 11"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This graph may look crowded.

That is itself a useful lesson: a graph that contains all available data is
not necessarily an effective graph.

We can instead select a smaller set of countries.

```r
selected_countries <- c(
  "Switzerland",
  "Germany",
  "France",
  "United Kingdom",
  "Sweden",
  "Italy"
)
```

Then:

```r
health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(country %in% selected_countries) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = education,
      y = good_health,
      group = country,
      linetype = country
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Educational gradients in self-rated health",
    subtitle = "Selected ESS countries, Round 11",
    linetype = "Country"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 2: Compare gradients

Look at the selected countries.

1. Is good health generally more common among respondents with higher
   education?
2. Is the gradient equally steep in every country?
3. Does Switzerland appear more or less unequal than the other countries?
4. Are there countries where overall health appears high but the educational
   gradient is nevertheless substantial?
:::

## Step 9: Calculate the absolute educational health gap

Graphs are useful, but we also want a numerical measure of inequality.

For each country, extract the health level of the low- and high-education
groups.

One convenient approach is to reshape the data.

First create separate low- and high-education datasets:

```r
health_low <- health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(education == "Low") %>%
  select(
    country,
    health_low = good_health
  )
```

```r
health_high <- health_by_country_education %>%
  filter(education == "High") %>%
  select(
    country,
    health_high = good_health
  )
```

Combine them:

```r
country_gaps <- health_low %>%
  inner_join(
    health_high,
    by = "country"
  )
```

Now calculate the absolute difference:

```r
country_gaps <- country_gaps %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap = health_high - health_low
  )
```

Inspect the result:

```r
country_gaps %>%
  arrange(desc(absolute_gap))
```

To express the difference in percentage points:

```r
country_gaps <- country_gaps %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap_pp = absolute_gap * 100
  )
```

Now the interpretation is straightforward.

For example:

> The proportion reporting good health is 12 percentage points higher among
> respondents with high education than among respondents with low education.

## Step 10: Visualise the absolute gaps

```r
ggplot(
  country_gaps,
  aes(
    x = reorder(country, absolute_gap),
    y = absolute_gap
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Absolute health gap",
    title = "Educational inequality in self-rated health",
    subtitle = "High education minus low education, ESS Round 11"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

This graph now answers a different question from our first country graph.

The first graph showed:

> **Which countries have better average health?**

This graph shows:

> **Which countries have larger educational health inequalities?**

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 3: Health levels versus health inequality

Compare the two country rankings.

1. Are the countries with the best average health also the countries with the
   smallest educational health gaps?
2. Where does Switzerland rank on average health?
3. Where does Switzerland rank on health inequality?
4. What does this tell you about the distinction between **population health**
   and **health inequality**?
:::

## Step 11: Calculate relative inequalities

As in Session 2, we should not rely only on absolute differences.

Calculate the relative ratio:

```r
country_gaps <- country_gaps %>%
  mutate(
    relative_ratio = health_high / health_low
  )
```

Inspect:

```r
country_gaps %>%
  arrange(desc(relative_ratio))
```

A value of `1` indicates no relative difference.

A value of `1.20`, for example, means that the prevalence of good health is
1.20 times as high in the high-education group as in the low-education group.

Now compare the country ranking based on:

- `absolute_gap`; and
- `relative_ratio`.

```r
country_gaps %>%
  select(
    country,
    health_low,
    health_high,
    absolute_gap_pp,
    relative_ratio
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(absolute_gap_pp))
```

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 4: Does the measure matter?

Do countries receive exactly the same ranking when you use:

- the **absolute difference**, and
- the **relative ratio**?

If not, why might the rankings differ?

Which measure would you report in a research paper?
:::

A strong answer is usually:

> **Both**, together with the underlying group-specific health levels.

## Part II: Comparing health inequalities over time

Cross-national comparison gives us one benchmark.

A second benchmark is **time**.

Suppose Switzerland has an educational health gap of 10 percentage points
today.

Was the gap smaller in the past?

Larger?

Or broadly unchanged?

We can examine this by comparing different rounds of the same survey.

For the ESS, we use:

- **ESS Round 7**; and
- **ESS Round 11**.

## Step 12: Import ESS Round 7

```r
ess7 <- read_dta("../../data/ESS7e02_3.dta")
```

Inspect the country variable:

```r
table(ess7$cntry)
```

Construct readable country names:

```r
ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  mutate(
    country = countrycode(
      cntry,
      origin = "iso2c",
      destination = "country.name"
    )
  )
```

## Step 13: Harmonise the health variable

The aim is to construct the health outcome in the same way in both rounds.

```r
ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  mutate(
    health_good = case_when(
      health %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1,
      health %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
```

Check the variable:

```r
table(ess7$health_good, useNA = "ifany")
```

The coding is now identical to the indicator we constructed for ESS Round 11:

- `1` = good or very good health;
- `0` = fair, bad or very bad health.

This consistency is essential. If we changed the definition of the outcome
between survey rounds, an apparent change over time could simply reflect a
change in measurement.

## Step 14: Harmonise education

We also construct the education groups in exactly the same way as for ESS
Round 11.

```r
ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      eisced %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Low",
      eisced %in% c(3, 4, 5) ~ "Medium",
      eisced %in% c(6, 7) ~ "High",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
    )
  )
```

Check the result:

```r
table(ess7$education, useNA = "ifany")
```

We now have comparable measures of:

> **self-rated health × education**

in both ESS rounds.

## Step 15: Compare Switzerland over time

We first return to Switzerland.

Calculate health by education in ESS Round 7:

```r
ch7 <- ess7 %>%
  filter(
    country == "Switzerland",
    !is.na(education)
  ) %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

And in ESS Round 11:

```r
ch11 <- ess11 %>%
  filter(
    country == "Switzerland",
    !is.na(education)
  ) %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Add a survey-round indicator and combine the estimates:

```r
ch7 <- ch7 %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 7")

ch11 <- ch11 %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 11")

ch_time <- bind_rows(ch7, ch11)
```

Inspect the result:

```r
ch_time
```

Visualise the educational gradients:

```r
ggplot(
  ch_time,
  aes(
    x = education,
    y = good_health,
    group = round,
    linetype = round
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = percent_format(),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Education",
    y = "Good or very good health",
    title = "Educational gradients in self-rated health in Switzerland",
    subtitle = "ESS Round 7 and ESS Round 11",
    linetype = "Survey round"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

<!-- EXERCISE -->

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 5: Has the Swiss gradient changed?

Compare the two survey rounds.

1. Has self-rated health improved or deteriorated in each educational group?
2. Is the educational gradient visible in both rounds?
3. Does the gradient appear steeper or flatter in the later round?
4. Can you tell from the graph whether the **absolute inequality** has changed?
5. What additional calculation would you need?
:::

## Step 16: Quantify change in the health gap

We can now calculate the absolute educational health gap separately for each
survey round.

```r
ch_gaps <- ch_time %>%
  filter(education %in% c("Low", "High")) %>%
  select(round, education, good_health) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = education,
    values_from = good_health
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap = High - Low,
    absolute_gap_pp = absolute_gap * 100,
    relative_ratio = High / Low
  )
```

Inspect the results:

```r
ch_gaps
```

You can now compare both measures directly.

For the absolute measure:

```r
ch_gaps %>%
  select(
    round,
    Low,
    High,
    absolute_gap_pp
  )
```

For the relative measure:

```r
ch_gaps %>%
  select(
    round,
    Low,
    High,
    relative_ratio
  )
```

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 6: Has health inequality changed?

Based on your results:

1. Has the **absolute educational health gap** increased or decreased?
2. Has the **relative educational health inequality** increased or decreased?
3. Do the two measures lead to the same conclusion?
4. What happened to the underlying health levels of the low- and
   high-education groups?

Write a short interpretation of no more than **three sentences**.

Do not simply state that inequality "increased" or "decreased". Specify the
measure you are referring to.
:::

This last point is important.

Instead of writing:

> Health inequality increased.

a more precise statement would be:

> The absolute difference in good self-rated health between respondents with
> high and low education increased from X to Y percentage points between the
> two ESS rounds.

The second statement tells the reader **what was measured, between whom, and
using which measure of inequality**.

## Step 17: Extend the comparison across countries

We can now combine the two dimensions of comparison:

> **How do educational health inequalities differ across countries, and how
> have they changed over time?**

Rather than examining Switzerland alone, repeat the calculation for several
countries that participated in both ESS rounds.

Start by calculating health by country and education in ESS Round 7:

```r
health_ess7 <- ess7 %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(country),
    !is.na(education)
  ) %>%
  group_by(country, education) %>%
  summarise(
    good_health = mean(health_good, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(health_good)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 7")
```

We already constructed the corresponding estimates for ESS Round 11:

```r
health_ess11 <- health_by_country_education %>%
  mutate(round = "ESS Round 11")
```

Combine them:

```r
health_over_time <- bind_rows(
  health_ess7,
  health_ess11
)
```

Select countries that occur in **both** rounds:

```r
countries_both <- health_over_time %>%
  distinct(country, round) %>%
  count(country) %>%
  filter(n == 2) %>%
  pull(country)
```

Keep only these countries:

```r
health_over_time <- health_over_time %>%
  filter(country %in% countries_both)
```

::: {.callout-note}
### Why restrict the comparison?

The set of countries participating in the ESS is not identical in every
round.

If we compared the average inequality across all countries in Round 7 with
the average across all countries in Round 11, a difference could arise simply
because the **composition of countries changed**.

Restricting the analysis to countries observed in both rounds makes the
comparison more meaningful.
:::

## Step 18: Calculate country gaps in both rounds

We now calculate the low–high education gap for every country and round.

```r
country_gaps_time <- health_over_time %>%
  filter(education %in% c("Low", "High")) %>%
  select(
    country,
    round,
    education,
    good_health
  ) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = education,
    values_from = good_health
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    absolute_gap = High - Low,
    absolute_gap_pp = absolute_gap * 100,
    relative_ratio = High / Low
  )
```

Inspect the result:

```r
country_gaps_time
```

We can now ask whether the educational health gap changed within each country.

```r
country_gaps_time %>%
  select(
    country,
    round,
    absolute_gap_pp,
    relative_ratio
  ) %>%
  arrange(country, round)
```

For a smaller set of countries:

```r
selected_countries <- c(
  "Switzerland",
  "Germany",
  "France",
  "Sweden"
)

country_gaps_time %>%
  filter(country %in% selected_countries)
```

<!-- EXERCISE -->

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 7: Compare change across countries

Choose **four countries** that appear in both survey rounds.

For each country, compare the absolute educational health gap between
ESS Round 7 and ESS Round 11.

Then answer:

1. Did inequality change in the same direction in all four countries?
2. Which country experienced the largest change?
3. Does the cross-national ranking remain stable over time?
4. What does this suggest about treating health inequality as a fixed
   characteristic of a country?
:::

## A note on survey weights

So far, we have concentrated on the analytical logic of comparison.

Survey estimates can also be affected by the survey design and by differences
in respondents' probability of being included in the sample. Surveys therefore
provide **weights** that can be used for particular types of analysis.

The ESS documentation provides detailed guidance on which weights should be
used for different purposes. The choice becomes especially important when we
move from estimating patterns within one country to comparing or combining
countries.

::: {.callout-note}
### For this session

Our main objective is to understand the logic of **cross-national and
over-time comparison**, rather than to develop a complete survey-weighting
strategy.

For your empirical project, however, you should check the documentation for
the survey and waves you use and justify your choice of weights. We will
discuss this when developing your individual analyses.
:::

## Part III: A second source of comparative evidence — the ISSP

The European Social Survey is not our only source of comparative data.

The **International Social Survey Programme (ISSP)** provides another
opportunity to examine health and health inequality across countries and over
time.

For this course, two datasets are particularly useful:

- the **ISSP Health and Health Care 2011** module; and
- the **ISSP Health and Health Care II 2021** module.

Because both modules focus explicitly on health, they contain measures that
are not available in every ESS round.

Import the datasets:

```r
issp11 <- read_dta("../../data/ZA5800_v3-0-0.dta")
issp21 <- read_dta("../../data/ZA8000_v2-0-0.dta")
```

Inspect them:

```r
dim(issp11)
dim(issp21)
```

The coding differs between the two ISSP datasets. This means that variables
must be inspected and harmonised carefully before making comparisons.

::: {.callout-important}
### Exercise 8: Inspect before you recode

Using `names()`, `table()` and `attr(..., "labels")`, identify in each ISSP
dataset:

1. the country variable;
2. the self-rated health variable;
3. the education variable; and
4. the survey weight.

Do **not** assume that the variable names or missing-value codes are identical
in 2011 and 2021.

Record your findings before proceeding.
:::

This is an important part of empirical research.

A harmonised dataset does not eliminate the need to understand how its
variables are constructed.

## ESS and ISSP are complementary — not interchangeable

The ESS and ISSP allow us to examine similar substantive questions, but they
should not simply be pooled together.

Differences may exist in:

- questionnaire wording;
- response categories;
- education classifications;
- survey years;
- participating countries;
- sampling procedures; and
- weighting.

If an inequality estimate differs between the ESS and ISSP, we therefore
cannot immediately conclude that health inequality itself changed.

The difference may partly reflect **measurement or survey design**.

::: {.definition}
**Comparability is an empirical assumption, not a property that comes
automatically with having two datasets.**

Before comparing estimates, ask whether the underlying concepts,
measurements, populations and survey procedures are sufficiently comparable
for the question you want to answer.
:::

## From description to explanation

At this point, we can describe substantial variation.

We can ask:

- Which countries have better average health?
- Which countries have larger educational health inequalities?
- Are inequalities larger in absolute or relative terms?
- Have inequalities changed over time?

But there is an important limit to what we have done.

Suppose we observe that educational health inequality is larger in Country A
than in Country B.

That observation does **not** tell us why.

Possible explanations might involve:

- differences in the composition of the population;
- labour-market conditions;
- income inequality;
- healthcare institutions;
- social policies;
- health behaviours;
- material living conditions;
- psychosocial factors; or
- other contextual differences.

Distinguishing these explanations requires a different analytical step.

> **Description tells us where inequalities exist. Explanation asks why they
> exist.**

We will return to explanations in Session 5.

Before doing so, however, Session 4 introduces another important question:
**how people themselves perceive and explain health inequalities.**

## Your empirical project

You now have the basic tools needed to formulate a genuinely comparative
research question.

A useful structure is:

> **How does [health outcome] vary by [dimension of inequality] across
> [countries and/or time]?**

Examples include:

> How does educational inequality in self-rated health vary across European
> countries?

> Did educational inequality in self-rated health change between two ESS
> rounds?

> Is the gender gap in self-rated health similar across countries?

> Does the association between subjective social position and health vary
> across countries?

For your own project, start thinking about four choices:

1. **Health outcome:** What aspect of health are you interested in?
2. **Dimension of inequality:** Between which groups or positions will you
   compare health?
3. **Comparative dimension:** Which countries and/or survey waves will you
   compare?
4. **Measure:** Will you use an absolute measure, a relative measure, or both?

::: {.callout-important}
### Prepare your research question

Write down **one possible comparative research question** for your empirical
project.

Then identify:

- the dataset you would use;
- your health outcome;
- your dimension of inequality;
- the countries and/or years you would compare; and
- the measure of inequality you would report.

You do not need to commit to this question yet. The purpose is to translate a
substantive interest into an empirical design.
:::

## Recap

In Sessions 2 and 3, we have moved from the concept of health inequality to
comparative empirical analysis.

You should now be able to distinguish between three questions:

> **How healthy is a population?**

> **How unequally is health distributed within that population?**

> **How do those inequalities vary across countries and over time?**

Several principles are worth retaining:

1. **Health levels and health inequalities are different quantities.** A
   healthier population is not necessarily a more equal population.
2. **Comparison provides a benchmark.** A health gap becomes more informative
   when we can compare it across countries or over time.
3. **The measure matters.** Absolute and relative inequalities can develop
   differently.
4. **Comparability must be examined.** Similar variable labels do not
   necessarily imply identical measurement.
5. **Description is not explanation.** Cross-national variation can generate
   hypotheses about why inequalities differ, but it does not by itself
   establish the causes.

The empirical sequence so far has therefore been:

> **Observe → measure → compare**

## Next session: How do people perceive and explain health inequalities?

So far, **we as researchers** have defined and measured health inequality.

In Session 4, we change perspective.

People also form their own judgements about why some groups are healthier than
others. They may attribute health differences to, for example, **individual
choices and behaviours** or to **social and structural circumstances**.

These explanations may matter for whether people regard health inequalities as
a problem and whether they support policies intended to address them.

The next session therefore asks:

> **How do people perceive and explain health inequalities?**

We will examine public perceptions and **causal attributions** of health
inequality and consider how these relate to judgements about inequality and
public policy.

This also introduces an important distinction that will remain with us
throughout the course:

> **Observing an inequality, explaining its causes, judging whether it is
> unfair, and deciding what policy should do about it are four different
> questions.**

### Reading for Session 4

Baute (2025), *Social Science & Medicine*, 117946.

Before the session, consider:

> If two social groups have different health outcomes, what information would
> you need before deciding **why** the difference exists — and whether it is
> **unfair**?
